review.notes: Built on the course: decision focus, BLUF, Pyramid Principle, MECE, SCQA and order, one-page memo, key numbers and context, chart choice, clutter, what/so what/now what, storyline, board paper, appendix. Fictional company.

content.company: Vantage Telecom Services (fictional), a regional telecom services company
content.briefing: You prepare what the CEO and the board read. This week: a memo asking for budget, a monthly update, a board paper and a presentation. Executives have little time; every message must lead to a decision.

variants.text: You need the CEO to approve Kz 40 m for new network towers by Friday. How does your email start?

choices.t: 'Please approve Kz 40 m for towers by Friday.'
choices.f: BLUF: the request in the first two lines. Reasons follow.

choices.t: 'Over the last three years our network...'
choices.f: History first buries the ask. The CEO stops reading.

choices.t: 'I hope you are well. Some updates below.'
choices.f: No decision is visible.

variants.text: Before writing anything for the CEO, what do you decide first?

choices.t: What the reader must do: decide, approve, note
choices.f: Decision focus shapes the whole message.

choices.t: How long the document should be
choices.f: Length follows purpose.
Format comes after purpose.

variants.text: Your arguments for the towers: 'coverage gaps', 'customer complaints', 'competitor coverage', 'complaints in the north'. What is wrong?

choices.f: Mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive. Merge the overlap.
Three to five is right. The problem is overlap.
Overlaps confuse and weaken the case.

variants.text: The CFO is sceptical about new spending. How do you order the memo?

choices.t: SCQA: context first, then the answer
choices.f: For sceptical readers, build agreement before the answer.
Works for busy or supportive readers; a sceptic may resist.
Detail before the point loses any reader.

variants.text: In SCQA, what is the 'Complication'?

choices.f: Situation, then what changed, then the question it raises, then the answer.
That is the Answer.
That is the Situation.

variants.text: What does the title of a one-page decision memo say?

choices.f: 'Approve Kz 40 m for northern towers' tells the reader everything.
A topic, not a decision.
Says nothing about the content.

variants.text: Your monthly update to the CEO. Which pattern fits?

choices.f: A short three-part version for updates and emails.

choices.t: A list of every task done
choices.f: Activity is not insight.
The CEO must do your thinking.

variants.text: The memo body: what comes right after the recommendation?

choices.t: Cost and timing, then key reasons
choices.f: Recommendation with cost and timing, then supporting points.
Background belongs low, briefly.
Questions undermine the ask.

variants.text: Your draft has 22 numbers. How many key numbers should the message carry?

choices.f: Start from the decision; keep only numbers that support it.
Too many numbers hide the message.
Executives need the key numbers.

variants.text: Revenue was Kz 940 m this month. How do you present it?

choices.f: Context gives meaning: variance in value and percent.
False precision; round to what matters.
Without comparison, good or bad is unclear.

variants.text: To show 12 months of churn rate, which chart?

choices.f: Trend over time.
Pies show shares, not trends.
Exact, but the trend is harder to see.

variants.text: Your chart has heavy gridlines, a border, a legend and 3D bars. What do you do?

choices.t: Remove clutter so ink shows data
choices.f: Tufte: most ink should show data.
More decoration hides the data.
Clutter slows the reader.

variants.text: 'Churn rose to 3.2%.' What turns this into a useful executive message?

choices.t: Add so what and now what
choices.f: 'Up from 2.4%; costs Kz 15 m a year; we propose a retention offer.'
Method does not tell them what to do.
Formatting is not meaning.

variants.text: To compare complaints across 6 regions, which chart?

choices.f: Comparing categories: sorted bars show ranking at once.
Lines imply time.
Hard to compare and distorted.

variants.text: You draft a 20-slide deck. How do you check the storyline?

choices.t: Read only the slide titles in order
choices.f: Action titles alone should tell the whole story.
Design is not story.
Length is not logic.

variants.text: A slide title reads 'Q3 results'. How do you improve it?

choices.t: 'Q3 profit beat plan by 8% on lower costs'
choices.f: An action title states the point.
Still a topic, not a message.
Says what it covers, not what it shows.

variants.text: A board paper should open with:

choices.f: Decision, discussion or information, and the executive summary.
Method belongs in the appendix.
Background comes later and briefly.

variants.text: Your team wants to add 30 pages of supplier data to the board paper.

choices.t: Appendix it, unless needed to decide
choices.f: Appendix discipline keeps the main paper short.

choices.t: Put it all in the main paper
choices.f: The decision gets lost in data.
Directors may want it; the appendix keeps it available.

variants.text: A before-and-after edit of your memo. What changed in the 'after'?

choices.t: Decision, cost and deadline moved first
choices.f: The before version put history first and the vague ask last.

choices.t: More history was added at the start
choices.f: That is the before version's mistake.

choices.t: The ask became softer and vaguer
choices.f: Clear asks get faster decisions.

variants.text: The CEO replies: 'What exactly do you need from me?' What went wrong?

choices.t: The request was not clear up front
choices.f: State the decision and deadline in the first lines.

choices.t: The CEO did not read carefully
choices.f: Busy readers skim; the writer must make it easy.
Length was not the problem; clarity was.
